lead: A Moody diagram is a chart of the Darcy friction factor f against Reynolds number Re, drawn on log-log axes, with one curve for each relative roughness ε/D. It exists because the Colebrook-White equation gives f only implicitly: f appears on both sides, so hand calculation needs trial and error. The chart turns that iteration into one visual read. Designers use it to size water mains, plant piping and air ducts, and to check friction head loss in the Darcy-Weisbach equation before choosing a pump.
prereq: You need 4.1 Reynolds experiment for Re and the laminar-turbulent split, and 4.3 Darcy-Weisbach equation for f and head loss.

blocks.text: The horizontal axis is Reynolds number Re on a log scale, usually from 10³ to 10⁷. The vertical axis is the Darcy friction factor f on a log scale, usually 0.008 to 0.1. Each curve is one value of relative roughness ε/D. Here ε is the average height of the pipe-wall roughness in metres, D is the internal diameter in metres, and ε/D is dimensionless. A smooth drawn tube is near ε/D = 0; a rusty steel main is nearer 0.01.

Some syllabi call it Moody's chart or Moody chart. The chart is a picture of the Colebrook-White equation, not a separate law. It applies to steady, fully developed, turbulent flow in a circular pipe. It says nothing about fittings, and nothing about laminar flow beyond one straight line.

Below Re ≈ 2000 the flow is laminar and every roughness curve collapses onto one straight line: f = 64/Re. On log-log paper this line falls with slope −1. Roughness has no effect because the viscous layer fills the pipe. Use 4.2 Hagen-Poiseuille here, not the turbulent curves.
Between Re ≈ 2000 and 4000 the flow is in the critical zone. Friction is uncertain and can jump between laminar and turbulent values. Designers avoid sizing a pipe to run in this band.

Above Re ≈ 4000 the curves separate. The lowest curve is the smooth pipe, ε/D = 0; for Re below about 10⁵ the Blasius form f = 0.316 Re^(−1/4) gives it. As Re rises the curves fan out: this is the transitionally rough zone, where both Re and ε/D matter. At high Re each curve flattens into the fully rough zone, where f depends only on ε/D and is nearly constant. There the viscous sublayer is thinner than the roughness bumps, so viscosity stops shielding them.

items: Compute Re = VD/ν, with V the mean velocity in m/s, D the diameter in m and ν the kinematic viscosity in m²/s.
Compute ε/D, using the same unit for roughness and diameter.
If Re < 2000, use f = 64/Re. If 2000 < Re < 4000, redesign the pipe.
For Re > 4000, enter the chart at Re on the horizontal axis, move vertically to the curve for ε/D, then read f on the vertical axis.
Confirm the read value with the Haaland approximation.

figure.caption: Two curves from the Haaland approximation: the smooth pipe and ε/D = 0.002, drawn from Re = 10⁴, where the correlation is valid. The rough pipe flattens into the fully rough zone where f depends only on ε/D; the smooth pipe keeps falling, more slowly as Re rises, and never becomes constant.

spec.aria: Two falling curves show friction factor against Reynolds number from 10⁴ to 10⁷ for a smooth pipe and for relative roughness 0.002.

examples.question: Water flows at V = 0.5 m/s through a pipe of diameter D = 200 mm and length L = 100 m. The kinematic viscosity is ν = 1×10⁻⁶ m²/s and the relative roughness is ε/D = 0.002. Read the friction factor from a Moody diagram and find the friction head loss h_f. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
steps: Compute Re = VD/ν = 0.5 × 0.2 / (1×10⁻⁶) = 1×10⁵. This is well above 4000, so the flow is turbulent and the chart applies.
Relative roughness is already given: ε/D = 0.002.
Enter the chart at Re = 10⁵, move up to the ε/D = 0.002 curve, and read f ≈ 0.025. The Haaland check gives 0.0250, so the read value is sound.
Write the Darcy-Weisbach equation: h_f = f (L/D)(V²/(2g)).
Multiply: h_f = 0.025 × 500 × 0.01274 = 0.159 m, that is about 0.16 m.
examples.answer: The friction factor is f ≈ 0.025 and the friction head loss is h_f ≈ 0.16 m of water.

traps: Using ε in mm but D in m, so ε/D comes out 1000 times too large. Convert both to the same unit first.
Using the laminar line f = 64/Re for a turbulent flow. That line belongs only below Re ≈ 2000.
Confusing the Darcy friction factor with the Fanning friction factor. The chart gives Darcy; Fanning is one quarter of it.
Reading a curve for the wrong ε/D instead of interpolating between the two nearest curves.
Designing a pipe to run in the critical zone 2000 < Re < 4000, where the chart gives no dependable value.

quiz.q: What quantities are plotted on the two axes of a Moody diagram?
quiz.a: Reynolds number Re on the horizontal axis (log scale) and Darcy friction factor f on the vertical axis (log scale). Each curve is one value of relative roughness ε/D.

quiz.q: Write the friction factor relation used in the laminar region of the chart.
quiz.a: f = 64/Re, valid for Re below about 2000 and independent of roughness.

quiz.q: Why is a chart needed at all when the Colebrook-White equation is known?
quiz.a: Colebrook-White is implicit: f appears inside the logarithm on the right side. Solving it by hand needs iteration. The chart stores the solution for many ε/D values, so one visual read gives f.

quiz.q: At Re = 10⁷ the curves for ε/D = 0.002 and 0.005 are almost flat. What does that mean for design?
quiz.a: The flow is fully rough, so f depends only on ε/D. Changing the flow rate hardly changes f, and head loss then varies almost as V².

quiz.q: Water flows with Re = 2×10⁵ in a pipe of relative roughness ε/D = 0.001. Estimate f from the chart.
Water at 20 °C (ν = 1×10⁻⁶ m²/s) flows at 2 m/s through a 100 mm diameter pipe, ε/D = 0.0005, L = 50 m. Find f and h_f.
Two pipes have the same ε/D = 0.002, but Re = 3×10⁴ and 3×10⁶. Which has the larger f, and why?
quiz.a: The pipe at Re = 3×10⁴, because it lies in the transitionally rough zone where the curves are still falling; at 3×10⁶ the curve is flat in the fully rough zone.

quiz.q: Why does the chart show no separate roughness curves in the laminar zone?
quiz.a: In laminar flow the viscous layer fills the whole pipe. Roughness bumps stay buried inside it and do not disturb the streamlines, so only viscous shear counts and f = 64/Re for every roughness.

beyond: Not for the exam. Design software such as pipe-network solvers iterates Colebrook-White directly and often uses explicit approximations like Swamee-Jain instead of a chart. Real roughness grows with age, corrosion and biofouling, so ageing mains are re-rated with a higher ε. For non-circular ducts the same chart is used with the hydraulic diameter in place of D.
